big: Two friends each put ₹1 lakh at 10%. One earns interest only on the ₹1 lakh. The other earns interest on interest too. After 20 years, the second has far more. Time makes the gap.

lines: Both get 10%. Why do the totals differ?
Simple interest is paid only on the original sum. Compound interest is paid on the sum plus past interest. The longer you wait, the wider the gap.

note: Made-up figures, for learning only. The rule works best between about 6% and 12%.

alt: Two bars comparing simple and compound growth over twenty years
caps: Simple adds the same amount every year.
Compound adds interest on past interest.
After 20 years, compound is more than double.

q: At 12% a year, about how long does money take to double by the Rule of 72?
why: 12 years would suit a rate of 6%.
3 years would need a rate near 24%.
24 years would suit a rate near 3%.

q: ₹1,00,000 at 10% for 3 years. How does the simple interest total compare with compound?
opts: It is the same as compound
why: Compounding gives more than simple, not less.
The two differ once interest earns interest.
₹1,10,000 is only one year of simple interest.

q: A loan at 18% compounds against the borrower. What does that show?
opts: Rates do not matter for loans here
why: Debts grow the same way savings do.
Many loans do compound on unpaid balances.
Higher rates make loans grow faster.

q: A client says the Rule of 72 gives exact answers. What is the right reply?
opts: It is exact at every rate used
It works only for loans taken out
It works only for gold and silver
why: It is not exact, at any rate. It does not fit the facts given.
It applies to any compounding growth. It does not answer what was asked.
It applies to any asset or debt that compounds. The details here point elsewhere.
The rule is a quick estimate that suits mid-range rates.

pts: Simple interest is on the original sum. Compound is on sum plus interest.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate.
Compounding works on loans and costs too.
